cards.b: The distance of open water the wind blows over; a longer fetch makes bigger waves.
Constructive: low, strong swash, deposit. Destructive: high, strong backwash, erode.
Waves force air into cracks in rock; pressure breaks the rock apart.
Waves hurl sand and pebbles at the cliff, wearing it away.
Waves hit the beach at an angle (swash), backwash returns straight down; material zig-zags along the coast.
Alternating hard and soft rock: soft rock erodes into bays; hard rock remains as headlands.
Gently sloping rock surface left at the base of a retreating cliff.
Crack becomes cave, erodes through to arch, roof collapses leaving stack, then stack collapses to stump.
Long narrow ridge of sand/shingle attached at one end, formed by longshore drift where the coast changes direction.
A spit that grows across a bay, enclosing a lagoon.
Warm water 23 to 29 degrees C, shallow, clear and salty water, sunlight, low sediment.
Warm water stresses corals so they expel their algae and turn white; they may die.
Prop roots for support, breathing roots for oxygen, salt-excreting leaves.
Protect coasts from waves, nursery for fish, habitat, timber, trap sediment and store carbon.
Hard: sea walls, groynes, rock armour. Soft: beach nourishment, dune regeneration, managed retreat.

short.q: Explain how headlands and bays form.
short.model: Where hard and soft rock alternate along a coast, the soft rock erodes faster and forms bays. The harder rock is left sticking out as headlands.
points: soft erodes faster to form bays; hard remains as headlands

short.q: Explain why coral reefs only grow in shallow water.
short.model: Corals contain algae that need sunlight to make food. Light only reaches shallow, clear water, so deeper water cannot support them.

short.q: Explain how mangrove forests protect coasts.
short.model: Their dense roots slow waves and absorb wave energy, reducing erosion and flooding. The roots also trap sediment, which stabilises the shoreline.

short.q: Explain one advantage of soft engineering over a sea wall.
short.model: Beach nourishment is far cheaper and looks natural, whereas a sea wall costs millions per kilometre. It also provides a beach for tourists.
points: comparison with sea wall cost or appearance

short.q: Explain how climate change threatens coral reefs.
short.model: Rising sea temperatures cause coral bleaching as corals expel their algae. Ocean acidification from CO2 also weakens coral skeletons.
points: acidification or sea-level change affects corals
